solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Like many Canaletto scenes without seeing what controls light (8,5)

annotation.surface: An art critic noting that Canaletto's canal views were painted as if by a man who could not see.
annotation.walkthrough: The art-history opening hides two plain adjectives, Venetian and blind, which together name a window fitting.
annotation.definitionFit: A Venetian blind's adjustable slats let you control how much light comes into a room.

entries.clue: Vehicle’s items stripped and disappearing (9)

indicatorNotes.stripped: something stripped has its outer covering taken off, so THINGS loses its first and last letters

blocks.note: THINGS (items) with its outer letters removed

annotation.surface: A van gets stripped of its contents by thieves and the goods vanish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stripped' suggests a vandalised van, but it strips the outside letters off a synonym for items; the ’s is read as 'is', not as a possessive.
annotation.definitionFit: Vanishing and disappearing are the same present participle.

entries.clue: Actor Paul embracing son Ed? (7)

indicatorNotes.embracing: to embrace is to put your arms round, so NEWMAN goes round S

annotation.surface: Paul Newman hugging his son, a boy called Ed.
annotation.walkthrough: Ed reads as the son's name, but it is the short form of editor, and the question mark flags that an editor is just one kind of newsman.
annotation.definitionFit: An editor, or ed, works in news, so is an example of a newsman.

entries.clue: Being controversially biased doesn’t unite, unfortunately (11)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: what happens unfortunately goes wrong, so the letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters, the apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A comment that divisive, one-sided talk fails to bring people together.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a fair point about partisan argument, so the fodder reads naturally as part of the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: A tendentious argument promotes one side of a disputed question.

entries.clue: Capital stored in Bank Arabia (6)

indicatorNotes.stored in: the answer is stored inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: Money kept in a Saudi bank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money in a bank; it is a capital city, Turkey's.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Turkey's seat of government is one capital city among many.

entries.clue: Lightening vessel’s stern during hauling ashore (9)

indicatorNotes.stern: the stern is the back of a ship, so it takes the last letter of vessel
indicatorNotes.during: the L happens during BEACHING, so it sits inside it

blocks.note: beaching a boat is hauling it up onto the shore

annotation.surface: A boat being lightened of its load while it is dragged up the beach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lightening' pretends to be making a boat less heavy; it means making something paler.
annotation.definitionFit: Bleaching lightens the colour of hair or cloth.

entries.clue: Pause beer licence when heads are lacking (12)

indicatorNotes.when heads are lacking: both words lose their heads, that is their first letters

blocks.note: PINT (a beer) without its first letter

annotation.surface: A pub drinker asking to stop the beer when the landlord's licence lapses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heads' sounds like the froth on a beer, but it means the first letters of both words; a pint is the usual British measure of beer.
annotation.definitionFit: An intermission is a pause between parts of a play or film.

entries.clue: Note introduced by present government (10)

indicatorNotes.introduced by: the note is introduced into DONATION, put inside it

blocks.note: mi is a note in do-re-mi

annotation.surface: A memo delivered by the current administration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as 'current', setting up 'present government'; it is a gift.
annotation.definitionFit: Domination is rule over others, a harsh sense of government.

entries.clue: Entry to Black Sea Russophobe endlessly disrupted (9)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: without its end, so RUSSOPHOBE loses its final E
indicatorNotes.disrupted: the remaining letters are thrown out of order

annotation.surface: A Russia-hater blocking access to the Black Sea.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is geopolitics, so the Russophobe seems to be doing the disrupting; really his own letters are what gets disrupted.
annotation.definitionFit: The Bosphorus is the strait at Istanbul through which ships enter the Black Sea.

entries.clue: Group reportedly outlawed (4)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: a report is spoken, so the answer sounds like the word that follows

annotation.surface: A news line that an organisation has been proscribed.
annotation.walkthrough: BANNED and BAND sound the same in most accents.
annotation.definitionFit: A band is a group, of musicians or of people generally.

entries.clue: Civil service publishers stop English lines and kill US reserve (10,6)

blocks.note: a station is a stop on a line
to off someone is American slang for killing them

annotation.surface: Government printers told to halt English lines of text and scrap an American reserve.
annotation.walkthrough: The Stationery Office (HMSO) is the British government's official publisher. 'US' marks OFF as American usage.
annotation.definitionFit: The Stationery Office publishes Acts of Parliament and other official papers for the civil service.

entries.clue: Hurry of Conservative quitting continent (5)

indicatorNotes.quitting: the C quits the word, leaving it

blocks.note: continent as an adjective means self-restrained, chaste

annotation.surface: A Tory leaving a continent in a rush.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Continent' looks like a landmass, and with 'Conservative quitting' it suggests Brexit, but it is the adjective meaning chaste.
annotation.definitionFit: Haste and hurry are both nouns for rushing.

entries.clue: Setting up tackle (7)

blocks.note: setting up a match or election is fixing its result in advance
a ship's tackle: its ropes, blocks and chains

annotation.surface: Preparing fishing tackle.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses hide behind a picture of an angler: 'setting up' as fixing a result, 'tackle' as a ship's ropes. RIGGING is both.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the verb for fraudulently fixing a contest, and the noun for the ropes that work a sailing ship's sails.

entries.clue: Closely examine youth coming up with my French and German gossip (13)

indicatorNotes.coming up: in a down clue, coming up means reading from bottom to top, so LAD reverses

blocks.note: to scan is to examine closely

annotation.surface: Scrutinising a young man who shows up with a Frenchman and a German, as a tabloid might.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My French' is a cue to translate: the French for 'my' is MON.
annotation.definitionFit: A scandalmonger is a gossip who spreads scandal.

entries.clue: Feeling certain abandoning cover is never advantageous (2-3)

indicatorNotes.abandoning cover: the word gives up its cover, its outside letters

blocks.note: KNOWING (feeling certain) without its outer letters K and G

annotation.surface: Advice that confidently breaking cover never pays, as a soldier or a hunted animal might learn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests shelter under fire; here it is the outer shell of the word KNOWING.
annotation.definitionFit: A no-win situation is one that can never turn out to your advantage.

entries.clue: Suspect leak involving port Arab’s desire to steal (11)

indicatorNotes.Suspect: a suspect item is dodgy, so LEAK's letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.involving: the rearranged letters involve, take in, the port and the Arab

blocks.note: an Omani is an Arab; the ’s joins it to the definition

annotation.surface: A suspicious leak at a harbour, where an Arab trader is thought to be pilfering.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as an adjective on leak and 'port' as a harbour; the answer's letters are cut from LEAK with PT OMANI tucked in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase of the medical term, from Greek kleptes, thief, plus mania, a compulsion.

entries.clue: Letter is returned by general manager before answer (5)

indicatorNotes.returned: something returned comes back the other way, so IS becomes SI
indicatorNotes.before: 'before' is positional: what precedes it in the clue is placed ahead of the A

annotation.surface: A letter being sent back by the general manager before he replies.
annotation.walkthrough: The office surface makes 'letter' correspondence; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the eighteenth character of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of S, is one letter among many.

entries.clue: Showing reflection resolved my crimes with time (9)

indicatorNotes.resolved: to resolve is to break down and settle afresh, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: t = time, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A prisoner who reflected on his offences and settled them by serving his time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Showing reflection' suggests remorse; here it is reflection in a mirror.
annotation.definitionFit: A symmetric shape is its own mirror image, showing reflection about an axis.

entries.clue: Country relocating first queen (4)

indicatorNotes.relocating first: the first letter is moved, here to the end

blocks.note: Iran, with its first letter I moved to the back

annotation.surface: A country moving its first queen elsewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First queen' looks like a single phrase; 'first' belongs with 'relocating', and 'queen' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A rani is an Indian queen or a raja's wife.

entries.clue: As some servants are free outside palace finally (8)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a comparison; read 'liveried' as describing servants who wear livery

indicatorNotes.outside: one word placed outside another wraps round it, so RID sits on either side of the E

blocks.note: to be, or are, is to live, exist

annotation.surface: Palace staff who are allowed to walk free at last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Are' looks like the verb of the definition; it is the wordplay's first piece, LIVE, in the sense of exist.
annotation.definitionFit: Liveried servants wear livery, the uniform of a great household.

entries.clue: Gradually provide rent money demanded in direct debit (4-4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the rent and the fee inside the direct debit, between its two Ds

blocks.note: DD = direct debit, a standing bank payment
a rent is a rip, a tear

annotation.surface: A landlord collecting rent in small monthly direct debits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is set up as housing money but is a tear. A direct debit is the British term for an automatic payment authorised from your bank.
annotation.definitionFit: To drip-feed something is to supply it bit by bit.

entries.clue: Soft brown coal failing to start fire (6)

indicatorNotes.failing to start: the word does not start: its first letter is lost

blocks.note: lignite is a soft brown coal

annotation.surface: Cheap coal that will not catch in the grate.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has the coal failing to start a fire, and that is literally what happens to the word LIGNITE.
annotation.definitionFit: To ignite something is to set it on fire; fire here is a verb.

entries.clue: Guardian’s empty editorial going after criminal clergyman? (11,5)

indicatorNotes.empty: an empty word has lost its contents, keeping its outer letters
indicatorNotes.going after: something going after another follows it, so EL comes at the end

blocks.note: a criminal is someone in a gang, so the criminal clergyman is a minister in gang
EditoriaL with its insides emptied out

annotation.surface: A dig at the Guardian newspaper's vacuous leader column chasing a crooked vicar.
annotation.walkthrough: The Guardian is a British newspaper, which makes 'editorial' look literal. The question mark flags reading 'criminal clergyman' as a minister in a gang.
annotation.definitionFit: A ministering angel is a kindly carer, a guardian figure watching over someone.

entries.clue: Freemason’s garment, article protecting master? (5)

indicatorNotes.protecting: AN protects PRO by going round it

blocks.note: a pro is a master of a craft

annotation.surface: A Masonic apron protecting a lodge master, with a question mark for the nod to Masonic ritual.
annotation.walkthrough: A Freemason's apron is a ceremonial garment, and an apron protects its wearer, so the whole surface points at the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Freemasons wear a ceremonial apron as part of their regalia.

entries.clue: Ohio feels Ukraine is mobilising very well (4,1,5,2,4)

indicatorNotes.mobilising: to mobilise is to set in motion, so the letters move about

annotation.surface: An American state's view of the war: Ukraine is mobilising well.
annotation.walkthrough: The geopolitical surface makes 'very well' look like approval of Ukraine; it is the definition of a set phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Getting on like a house on fire means getting on very well.

entries.clue: Infuriating confining work in a career (9)

indicatorNotes.confining: GALLING confines OP, holding it inside

annotation.surface: Someone finding their job maddening.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like a job; as a verb it means to rush headlong, so 'in a career' is at full tilt.
annotation.definitionFit: A horse in a career is charging along, galloping.

entries.clue: Surveying of throne supported by monarch (7)

indicatorNotes.supported by: in a down clue the supporting word sits underneath, so KING comes after LOO

blocks.note: throne is jokey slang for the toilet; loo is the British word

annotation.surface: A king surveying his realm from the throne.
annotation.walkthrough: The regal surface makes 'throne' a royal seat; it is the lavatory, which the British call the loo.
annotation.definitionFit: Surveying and looking both mean casting your eyes over something.

entries.clue: Plug small type of hat (7)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
a topper is a top hat

annotation.surface: Promoting a small kind of hat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plug' reads as a verb, to advertise; it is a noun, a bung.
annotation.definitionFit: A stopper plugs the neck of a bottle.

entries.clue: Movement perhaps runs working party (5)

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

annotation.surface: A political movement run by a working party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Movement' looks political next to 'working party'; it is a section of a symphony, and 'perhaps' warns that a rondo is only one kind.
annotation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form often used for the last movement of a sonata or concerto.

entries.clue: Number one’s ascendant variety of pop in offensive (7)

indicatorNotes.ascendant: rising, which in a down clue means reading upward, so EMO turns round

blocks.note: one = I, ’s = is, leaving the S

annotation.surface: A chart-topping pop style that people find repugnant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Number one' is set up as a chart hit; it splits into NO and the I of 'one’s'.
annotation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive, especially of a smell.

entries.clue: Sample mix by orchestral division (5,7)

blocks.note: a cross is a mix, as in a hybrid breed
the strings or brass are sections of an orchestra

annotation.surface: A sound engineer mixing a sample of one orchestral section.
annotation.walkthrough: The music-studio surface makes 'sample' and 'mix' recording terms; here they are a representative selection and a hybrid.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a slice that represents the whole, as in polling a cross-section of voters.

entries.clue: Freely given running account includes what’s regularly occurring in pulpit (13)

indicatorNotes.includes: COMMENTARY includes the letters inside it
indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, every other letter

blocks.note: a running commentary is a live account

annotation.surface: A preacher giving a free, running account of what happens week to week in the pulpit.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a sermon; 'running account' is a sports commentary.
annotation.definitionFit: Complimentary tickets or drinks are given free.

entries.clue: Rather dull yokel in this novel (8)

indicatorNotes.in: HICK goes in the rearranged THIS
indicatorNotes.novel: novel means new, so THIS is made into a new arrangement

blocks.note: a hick is a country bumpkin

annotation.surface: A reviewer calling the country bumpkin in this book a bit of a bore.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as a book, which makes 'dull' a review; it is an adjective meaning new, telling you to rearrange THIS.
annotation.definitionFit: Thick means stupid, and thickish is rather stupid, rather dull.

entries.clue: Loud and clear resolution restricting ousting leader (10)

indicatorNotes.restricting: the word is restricted, cut short to its first three letters
indicatorNotes.leader: the ousted leader is the first letter, H

blocks.note: RESolution cut short; res is also the usual short form, as in screen res
hOUNDING, as in hounding out (ousting), with its leader dropped

annotation.surface: A decisive vote on a motion that limits the removal of a party leader.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as party politics, a motion curbing a leadership challenge. The mechanics are loose: ousting is HOUNDING (out), which loses its leading letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: literally echoing loudly, and figuratively emphatic, as in a resounding no.

entries.clue: Rely on ace, say, turning up? Extremely usual with a sucker? (5,7)

indicatorNotes.turning up: in a down clue, turning up means reading upward, so CARD is reversed
indicatorNotes.Extremely: only the extremes of usual, its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.with: the A joins on at the end

blocks.note: to count on is to rely on
an ace is an example of a CARD, reversed

annotation.surface: A card player trusting an ace to turn up, like any gambling sucker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' seems to mean a dupe at the card table; it is a bloodsucker, and the question mark flags the pun. 'Rely on' is COUNT because count on means rely on.
annotation.definitionFit: Count Dracula, Bram Stoker's vampire, sucks blood.

entries.clue: Fern, Miranda, he and I go travelling (10)

indicatorNotes.go travelling: letters that go travelling move to new places

annotation.surface: A roll call of friends, Fern, Miranda and two others, setting off on a trip.
annotation.walkthrough: Fern reads as a woman's name among the travellers; it is the plant, the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Maidenhair is a delicate fern with fan-shaped fronds.

entries.clue: Eclipse’s beginning — sun disc’s gobbled up (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning: the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the Aten was the sun disc worshipped in ancient Egypt

annotation.surface: The start of an eclipse, when the sun seems to be swallowed.
annotation.walkthrough: The Aten was the Egyptian god shown as the disc of the sun. The surface's eclipse really does look like the sun being gobbled up.
annotation.definitionFit: Eaten and gobbled up are both past participles for consumed.

entries.clue: Promise dispute over complete rowing crew covering house name (4,2,6)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so ROW reads backwards
indicatorNotes.covering: FOUR covers HO and N, going round them

blocks.note: to do a job is to complete it
a four is a rowing boat and its crew

annotation.surface: A row among a rowing crew about a pledge to finish the race, with a college house name thrown in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' tempts you towards a ROW; the dispute is the ROW, and the rowing crew is a FOUR.
annotation.definitionFit: Giving your word of honour is making a solemn promise.

entries.clue: Whence book may be had that’s readily available (3-3-5)

blocks.note: the literal sense: where a book is picked from in a library or shop
ready-made and in stock, not made to order

annotation.surface: Where a library book can be taken from.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is the literal place a book comes from, off the shelf; the second is the phrase's figurative sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Off-the-shelf products are standard and available at once.

entries.clue: Dog turned irrational eating junk food that’s starchy (6,4)

indicatorNotes.eating: POOCH eats TAT, taking it inside

blocks.note: tat is British slang for cheap junk

annotation.surface: A dog gone mad from wolfing down junk food.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Junk food' looks like a unit and so a definition; 'junk' is TAT and 'food' starts the definition. PI is the classic irrational number.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: fried slices of potato, a starchy vegetable, eaten as a snack (the British call them crisps).

entries.clue: Pollution cancelling Book Day (5)

indicatorNotes.cancelling: the B is cancelled, struck out

annotation.surface: A protest cancelling World Book Day because of pollution.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book Day' reads as a single event, but Book is the letter to lose and Day stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Light means daytime, as in 'while it's still light'.

entries.clue: Not recognised as variable (7)

blocks.note: said of a face or name nobody can place
in algebra, a letter such as x standing for a value still to be found

annotation.surface: Someone whose status is uncertain goes unrecognised.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Variable' reads as an adjective, changeable; it is a noun from algebra, where x is the unknown.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the adjective for unfamiliar or unidentified, and the algebra noun for a quantity to be solved for.

entries.clue: City child confused with life (9)

indicatorNotes.confused: the letters are confused, mixed together

annotation.surface: A city child bewildered by life.
annotation.walkthrough: Lichfield is a small cathedral city in Staffordshire, in the English Midlands.
annotation.definitionFit: Lichfield has city status thanks to its cathedral.

entries.clue: Form of verse that’s no good encountered in traditional learning (4,5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'encountered in' places NG and MET inside the learning, splitting LORE

annotation.surface: A poetry form judged worthless when met in the classical syllabus.
annotation.walkthrough: The literary surface makes 'traditional learning' a school subject; it is simply LORE.
annotation.definitionFit: Long metre is a hymn stanza of four eight-syllable lines.

entries.clue: Willingly avoid party outside for old people (2,7)

blocks.note: without meaning outside is an old usage, as in 'within and without'

annotation.surface: Skipping a party held outdoors for pensioners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For old people' looks like the party's guest list; it marks WITHOUT as the old-fashioned word for outside.
annotation.definitionFit: To do without something is to manage without it, choosing to forgo it.

entries.clue: Split position after I’m backing argument (16)

indicatorNotes.backing: going backwards, so I'M becomes MI
indicatorNotes.after: the split and the position come after MI

annotation.surface: Someone backing one side of a split and so starting a row.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split' and 'backing' read as taking sides in a quarrel; both are wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A misunderstanding is a mild word for a disagreement or argument.

entries.clue: What might need pumping in pipes to machine? (7)

annotation.definition: What might need pumping in pipes to machine?

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits in the words that follow

annotation.surface: A plumber wondering what needs pumping through the pipes to a machine.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a stomach pump is a hospital procedure, and the stomach is fed by pipes.
annotation.definitionFit: A stomach may need pumping after poisoning, and it sits at the end of the gullet's pipework.

entries.clue: Explain hugging a daughter’s inseparable companion (6)

indicatorNotes.hugging: SHOW hugs A and D, wrapping round them

blocks.note: to show is to explain, demonstrate

annotation.surface: A parent explaining why their daughter is always hugging her best friend.
annotation.walkthrough: The domestic picture makes the companion a friend; a shadow follows you everywhere.
annotation.definitionFit: A shadow is someone who follows another everywhere, an inseparable companion.

entries.clue: End of term somewhat subdued at Eton (3,4)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: only some of the words are used

annotation.surface: Pupils at Eton, the English public school, rather quiet as the school term ends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Term' looks like a school term at Eton; it is a pregnancy, whose end is the due date.
annotation.definitionFit: A baby's due date marks the end of the mother's term of pregnancy.

entries.clue: Oxygen taken after jumper’s exercise (6)

indicatorNotes.taken after: the O is placed after CARDI

blocks.note: a cardi (cardigan) is a British jumper, a knitted top

annotation.surface: Oxygen needed after a high-jumper's workout.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' reads as an athlete; it is the British word for a sweater, here a cardigan.
annotation.definitionFit: Cardio is aerobic exercise that works the heart.

entries.clue: Kissing and cuddling without roughly, aimlessly playing (8)

indicatorNotes.without: 'without' means lacking, so the letters for roughly are taken away from the kissing and cuddling

blocks.note: ca = circa, roughly; removed from the front

annotation.surface: A couple kissing and cuddling gently, not roughly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' seems to describe the canoodling, but it is CA, short for circa.
annotation.definitionFit: Noodling is playing an instrument idly, improvising aimlessly.

entries.clue: Monster initially like any monster in antiquity (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the initial letters of the words that follow

blocks.note: the first letters of Like Any Monster In Antiquity

annotation.surface: A description of a creature from ancient myth.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay also describes the answer: a lamia is a monster of antiquity, from Greek myth.
annotation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Lamia was a child-devouring monster, part woman, part serpent.

entries.clue: Clubs fuss around ending music (4)

indicatorNotes.around: turned around, so ADO reads backwards

annotation.surface: Nightclubs kicking up a fuss about the music stopping.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests nightlife; it is the card suit abbreviated to C.
annotation.definitionFit: A coda is the closing passage of a piece of music.

entries.clue: What could stop benefit game after team member’s accepting Ecstasy (5,4)

indicatorNotes.accepting: MAN'S accepts E, taking it inside
indicatorNotes.after: the game comes after the rest

blocks.note: a man in a team; the ’s gives the S
a Test is an international cricket match

annotation.surface: A player caught taking Ecstasy who could lose his match fee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Benefit' looks like a sports benefit match; it is welfare payments, which a means test can deny.
annotation.definitionFit: A means test checks a claimant's income and can stop their benefit.

entries.clue: Visit gets me rising in protest (4)

indicatorNotes.gets: DO gets ME, taking it inside
indicatorNotes.rising: in a down clue rising means reading upward, so ME becomes EM

blocks.note: to do a place is to visit it as a tourist

annotation.surface: Someone joining a march when they visit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rising' feels like a revolt to go with the protest; it turns ME upward.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British shortening of demonstration, a public protest.

entries.clue: Danger signal in the style of room (5)

blocks.note: à la = in the style of

annotation.surface: A warning light designed to match the décor of a room.
annotation.walkthrough: À la is French borrowed into English, meaning in the manner of.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bell, siren or call that warns of a threat, from Italian all'arme, to arms.

entries.clue: Dicky hated unisex not being fully used (11)

indicatorNotes.Dicky: dicky is British slang for unsound or faulty, so the letters are faulty

annotation.surface: A man called Dicky who hated unisex fashions.
annotation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a man's name; it is the British adjective for shaky or faulty, as in a dicky heart.
annotation.definitionFit: A rare adjective: in- plus exhausted in its sense of used up, so still with some left.

entries.clue: Who encouraged love poetry at an average rate but not modern? (5)

indicatorNotes.but not: 'but not' means except, so the modern part is taken away

blocks.note: moderato is the musical marking for moderate speed
MOD = modern, removed from the front

annotation.surface: Asking which old muse supported love poetry at a steady rate, before modern times.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At an average rate' reads like a pay grade; it is the tempo marking moderato.
annotation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of love poetry, who inspired poets.

entries.clue: At sea, cry years over dismissal (2-5-2)

blocks.note: getting the heave-ho is being dismissed

annotation.surface: Someone lost and weeping for years after being sacked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' looks like 'confused'; it goes with 'cry' to make the definition, a sailors' chant.
annotation.definitionFit: Yo-heave-ho is the sailors' cry when hauling together on a rope.

entries.clue: Large excellent black coffee drunk in part as something improving health (7,6)

indicatorNotes.drunk: a drunk word staggers about, so COFFEE's letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.in: 'in part' places everything else inside PT, between its two letters

annotation.surface: A big excellent black coffee, drunk partly because you think it does you good.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a coffee order, and 'drunk' reads as swallowed; it tells you to scramble COFFEE.
annotation.definitionFit: The placebo effect is an improvement in health caused by belief in a treatment rather than the treatment.
